stimulus.title: Social Science: The Paths People Choose
stimulus.text:
Walk across almost any college campus or city park and you will find them: narrow ribbons of bare earth cutting diagonally across the grass, worn smooth by thousands of shoes. Landscape architects call them desire paths. They appear wherever the route people want to take differs from the route a designer has paved for them, and they are, in their quiet way, a form of protest. Each one records a small decision made again and again by people who will never meet: the paved path goes around, but I am going through.

For a long time, the standard response to desire paths was to fight them. Groundskeepers put up fences, planted hedges, and posted signs asking pedestrians to keep off the grass. These measures rarely worked for long. A sign can be ignored, and a hedge, sooner or later, develops a gap exactly the width of a person. The trouble was not that people were careless. It was that the paved paths had been laid out according to what looked orderly on a drawing, with neat right angles and symmetrical loops, rather than according to where people actually needed to go.

Some designers began to wonder whether the paths might be useful rather than merely annoying. If thousands of people independently chose the same shortcut, perhaps they were collectively solving a problem the designers had missed. A few universities have taken this idea to its logical conclusion. Rather than paving walkways when a new building opens, they plant the surrounding area with grass and wait. Over a season or two, students wear their own routes into the lawn. Only then do the planners pour concrete, following the lines the walkers have drawn. The result can look a little unusual from above, with walkways that branch at odd angles, but the grass on either side stays green because no one has a reason to leave the path.

The approach has an obvious appeal. It costs little, it produces paths that people will actually use, and it treats pedestrians as experts in their own movement. It also reflects a broader shift in how planners think about public space. Older approaches often began with a fixed vision and expected people to conform to it. Newer ones are more likely to start by observing behavior, such as counting foot traffic, watching where people pause, and noticing which benches go unused, and to treat that behavior as evidence rather than as a problem to be corrected.

Still, desire paths are not always a reliable guide. A shortcut that saves a few seconds on a dry afternoon may become a mud slide in the spring, and a route that suits students in a hurry may be too steep or uneven for someone using a wheelchair or pushing a stroller. Some paths form simply because one person cut a corner and others followed the visible trail, not because the route was especially efficient. In those cases, the path records habit more than need.

There is also the question of what gets lost. A lawn crisscrossed with paths is a lawn with less grass, and in some places the ground being worn away is not ornamental turf but fragile habitat. In national parks, rangers work hard to keep visitors on marked trails precisely because shortcuts can erode hillsides and damage plants that take decades to recover. What counts as a sensible shortcut in a city park may be a scar in a wilderness.

Perhaps the most useful lesson of desire paths, then, is not that the crowd is always right but that the crowd is always communicating. A worn strip of earth is information. It tells designers where their plans and people's needs have come apart. Sometimes the right response is to pave the path; sometimes it is to make the official route more appealing; occasionally it is to put up the fence after all. But ignoring the message entirely is rarely the right choice.

choices.text: fence off new lawns until students agree to use only the paved walkways
choices.rationale: Fences are part of the old approach of fighting the paths.

Perhaps the most useful lesson of desire paths, then, is not that the crowd is always right but that the crowd is always communicating. A worn strip of earth is information. It tells designers where their plans and people's needs have come apart. Sometimes the right response is to pave the path; sometimes it is to make the official route more appealing; occasionally it is to put up the fence after all. But ignoring the message entirely is rarely the right choice.

stimulus.title: Social Science: The Paths People Choose
stimulus.text:
Walk across almost any college campus or city park and you will find them: narrow ribbons of bare earth cutting diagonally across the grass, worn smooth by thousands of shoes. Landscape architects call them desire paths. They appear wherever the route people want to take differs from the route a designer has paved for them, and they are, in their quiet way, a form of protest. Each one records a small decision made again and again by people who will never meet: the paved path goes around, but I am going through.

For a long time, the standard response to desire paths was to fight them. Groundskeepers put up fences, planted hedges, and posted signs asking pedestrians to keep off the grass. These measures rarely worked for long. A sign can be ignored, and a hedge, sooner or later, develops a gap exactly the width of a person. The trouble was not that people were careless. It was that the paved paths had been laid out according to what looked orderly on a drawing, with neat right angles and symmetrical loops, rather than according to where people actually needed to go.

Some designers began to wonder whether the paths might be useful rather than merely annoying. If thousands of people independently chose the same shortcut, perhaps they were collectively solving a problem the designers had missed. A few universities have taken this idea to its logical conclusion. Rather than paving walkways when a new building opens, they plant the surrounding area with grass and wait. Over a season or two, students wear their own routes into the lawn. Only then do the planners pour concrete, following the lines the walkers have drawn. The result can look a little unusual from above, with walkways that branch at odd angles, but the grass on either side stays green because no one has a reason to leave the path.

The approach has an obvious appeal. It costs little, it produces paths that people will actually use, and it treats pedestrians as experts in their own movement. It also reflects a broader shift in how planners think about public space. Older approaches often began with a fixed vision and expected people to conform to it. Newer ones are more likely to start by observing behavior, such as counting foot traffic, watching where people pause, and noticing which benches go unused, and to treat that behavior as evidence rather than as a problem to be corrected.

Still, desire paths are not always a reliable guide. A shortcut that saves a few seconds on a dry afternoon may become a mud slide in the spring, and a route that suits students in a hurry may be too steep or uneven for someone using a wheelchair or pushing a stroller. Some paths form simply because one person cut a corner and others followed the visible trail, not because the route was especially efficient. In those cases, the path records habit more than need.

There is also the question of what gets lost. A lawn crisscrossed with paths is a lawn with less grass, and in some places the ground being worn away is not ornamental turf but fragile habitat. In national parks, rangers work hard to keep visitors on marked trails precisely because shortcuts can erode hillsides and damage plants that take decades to recover. What counts as a sensible shortcut in a city park may be a scar in a wilderness.

Perhaps the most useful lesson of desire paths, then, is not that the crowd is always right but that the crowd is always communicating. A worn strip of earth is information. It tells designers where their plans and people's needs have come apart. Sometimes the right response is to pave the path; sometimes it is to make the official route more appealing; occasionally it is to put up the fence after all. But ignoring the message entirely is rarely the right choice.
